speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: As a country, we have done well to provide the conditions for Singaporeans to enjoy increased longevity.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: However, one of the issues that may arise in old age is the loss of cognitive ability.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: This means that out of 100 elderly persons, 10 might have dementia at some point.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: I understand that Minister Vivian, when he introduced the Mental Capacity Act (MCA) a number of years ago, asked the same question – imagine all of us in this House here, quite a number of us will have dementia.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The question is, will we be ready when it happens to us?

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The loss of cognitive ability is, of course, not an issue that only affects older Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Accidents and illnesses may rob us of our ability to make decisions at any time.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The MCA is a key statute that empowers Singaporeans to plan ahead and make their wishes known.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: It is writing into law what we feel is in our bones – that is, to enable us to live meaningful and dignified lives, even if we lose our mental capacity.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: This is a legal instrument that allows each of us to choose someone we trust to make decisions for us, if and when we are no longer able to do so.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The entrusted proxy decision-maker, who is usually a family member, is called the "donee".

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: It also enables us to act in the best interests of our incapacitated loved ones.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We can apply to Court to be appointed as "deputies" to act for our loved one who has lost capacity but has no LPA.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The MCA is undergirded by three fundamental principles.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: First, we respect the choices of a person who has mental capacity.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We cannot assume a donor lacks capacity just because we think he or she could have made a better decision.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: This is so, even in respect of the choice of donee.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Third, the state must build a system with sufficient checks and balances to protect individuals who lack mental capacity from abuse or having their interest compromised.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: This has to be done without making access to LPAs too restrictive, which will defeat the purpose of the LPA in the first place.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The MCA has been in operation for about six years now.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: More of us need to make our LPAs.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Over these past six years, we have also implemented the MCA framework.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We have learnt useful lessons and it is timely to amend the MCA to meet emerging needs and strengthen its protection capability.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: In preparing this Bill, we have sought feedback from organisations in the legal, banking, insurance, medical and social service sectors, as well as members of the public.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: They have all provided very valuable insights and supported the proposed enhancements.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We also studied the experience in some countries with a longer history of similar legislation, such as the UK and the US, particularly in Florida.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: These jurisdictions also have a more developed private sector to serve as professional donees and deputies.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Besides these legislative amendments, we are also undertaking some policy initiatives that complement these amendments.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: I will elaborate more on these initiatives later.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Families are a key source of support for our elderly.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: A large majority of donees and deputies today are family members.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: They have stepped up out of love and concern for the person whom they have been appointed for, and this is as it should be.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: However, there will be a small and increasing number of elderly singles or childless elderly couples who may not have family members or close friends to rely on to be their proxy decision-makers.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: One MSF officer recently recounted to me her visit to a Dementia Day Care Centre.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Some of the elderly there were in the early stages of dementia and were still lucid.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Among them were a few single elderly with no relatives or close friends.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: They had worked hard and saved carefully for their old age.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: But they were deeply anxious, as they had no suitable person to nominate as their donee.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: They were actually quite afraid about what would happen to their dignity and quality of life when they lose capacity.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: They did not want to become wards of the state.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The officer told me that she cannot forget the worry and anxiety she saw in their eyes.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The community has stepped forward to work with MSF on supporting a small number of such elderly who had no family support.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: About one-and-a-half years ago, we started work with public-spirited volunteers from the medical, legal, accounting and social work professions to form a panel of deputies.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Once appointed by the Court as deputies, they helped to manage the affairs of the elderly persons and ensure that their finances are used for their care by setting up a trust with the MSF-funded Special Needs Trust Company (SNTC).

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: This arrangement – which is in the pilot stage with five test cases – has worked well so far.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: In one case, the elderly lady who was helped could use her finances to upgrade to a better room in a nursing home.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: She was even more joyous that she could resume attending her weekly church service, as she could now pay for her transport fees and other incidental costs.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The number of elderly without next-of-kin will increase.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: It empowers such elderly, especially those with assets, to have a choice and to give more complex instructions as to their care should they lose capacity.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Professional deputies are those who can provide deputyship services for a fee.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: They are appointed by the Court to act on behalf of individuals with assets who lack mental capacity and do not have family members or friends who can play the role of a deputy.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We envisage that professional deputies would include licensed trust companies, as well as professionals, such as lawyers and accountants.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: They must not be related to the person they have been appointed for.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: A professional deputy must be registered with the Public Guardian (PG).

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We have not finalised the details of the registration framework and will be consulting stakeholders extensively before we do so.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: However, let me share some of our initial thoughts on how we think it will work.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: To be considered for registration, the professional deputy should not be a bankrupt.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: He should also have sufficient knowledge of the MCA and what a deputy's role and responsibilities are.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The PG will be empowered to cancel the registration of a professional deputy, if certain events occur.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: One such event could be that the professional deputy becomes bankrupt or is convicted of an offence involving fraud or dishonesty.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Upon cancelling registration, the PG can apply to Court for the professional deputy's appointment to be revoked.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Unlike deputies, who are appointed by the Court after the individual has lost mental capacity, professional donees are chosen by the individual when he still has capacity.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Licensed trust companies are regulated by MAS under the Trust Companies Act.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The passing of these amendments will just be the first step towards regulating the professional deputy and donee sector.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We will consult the various stakeholders extensively before finalising the details.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: But the key principle behind the framework is this – mentally incapacitated persons are extremely vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Hence, the regulatory framework must ensure that a professional donee or deputy is competent, of suitable character and accountable to the relevant authorities for what he does.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Members may have concerns about the fees that professional deputies and donees will charge and what will be done for those who need these services but are without means.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: I assure members that for these individuals, MSF will work with partners to ensure that pro bono or low-cost services are available, just like what we did in the pilot.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Some may also ask why the Government does not provide doneeship and deputyship services.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: I do not think it is possible nor wise for the Government to be everyone's donee or deputy.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: It is certainly not appropriate for the Government to manage the assets and personal welfare matters of private individuals.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Our role is to put in place an effective regulatory framework that enables these services to be provided, while protecting the interests of those without mental capacity.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Members of the House will know of some of the cases we have encountered, where there were concerns about exploitative behaviour by donees.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Some Members have also offered suggestions on how to improve the LPA framework to prevent such abuses from recurring.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: I am relieved to say that these cases actually only form a small minority and the law has taken its course in protecting the donors.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Nonetheless, we have reviewed the matter and propose two key amendments to the MCA.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The aim is to enable pre-emptive action, so that individuals who lack mental capacity can be better protected against abuse by their donees or deputies.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: For instance, the risk of abuse would be significant, if the donee or deputy is convicted of an offence involving dishonesty or fraud.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: This offence could have been committed against some other person and not simply just the donor.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: With the proposed amendments, the Court can pre-emptively revoke the donee's or deputy's appointment and eliminate chances of exploitation from happening.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Say, for example, a deputy has been charged with an offence involving fraud or dishonesty and there is a real risk that he will dissipate the assets of the person who lacks mental capacity.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We want to be able to suspend the deputy's powers while investigations are on-going.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We must have a prior or concurrent Court application to revoke the deputyship order.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: However, it is not appropriate to apply for a revocation as the deputy has only been charged, but not yet found guilty and convicted by the Courts.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We can, thus act pre-emptively and, hopefully, in a timely manner.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: I will use the facts that are already known to the public about the case involving Mdm Chung and former China tour guide, Yang Yin.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: But I will just be using the case as an illustration.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: I will not comment on any aspect of the case which is still on-going in the Courts and I will also not comment further than what I will say below.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: As is public knowledge, Yang Yin was charged with offences of falsifying receipts at his company and criminal breach of trust of monies belonging to Mdm Chung.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: In these kinds of cases, there is a cause for concern because the donee has been charged with an offence involving fraud or dishonesty and there is a risk of the donor's property being dissipated if nothing is done.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Once investigations are complete and if the donee is eventually convicted of the offences, the Court may then revoke the LPA.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Some may suggest that we should be even more pre-emptive.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Nip the problem in the bud at the LPA-making stage.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: For instance, make it mandatory for donors to inform their family members about their LPA, or give the PG the power to refuse the registration of an LPA if he suspects that the proposed donee is not a suitable candidate, or is not a family member.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: But I think it is important that we must remember that one of the fundamental principles of the MCA is that the decisions of a person who has mental capacity must be respected.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Where do we draw the line if we do not respect that person's autonomy?

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The officers at OPG have encountered cases where both sides of the same donor's family have competing claims.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: In one case, the donor's daughter alleged that her brother had unduly influenced their mother to make an LPA appointing him as donee and restricted her access to their mother.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: According to her, he was eyeing their mother's property.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: On the other hand, the brother claimed that the relationship between mother and daughter was so estranged that their mother did not want to see her and never wanted to appoint his sister as a donee.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: So, who is right and who is wrong?

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: In another case, a donor appointed a friend to be his donee, even though he had three children as well as extended family.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: His children complained to OPG, but it turned out that there was no evidence of undue influence.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: In fact, the children did not appear to play a big part in the donor's life at all.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: And the donee turned out to be his close childhood friend whom he trusts.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: So, these cases illustrate that each case has its unique circumstances.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: It is not for the PG to decide against a donor's wish.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Neither is the PG the arbiter of another's choices, such as in appointing one child as donee and not the other.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Doing so will compromise PG's ability to render objective reports to the Courts when called upon to do so.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The PG only steps in and, rightly so, when there is no family or friend to intervene for a donor who has lost capacity and the donee or deputy is not acting in his best interests.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We believe that this would enhance family support if the LPA needs to be activated.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Besides making amendments to better protect individuals who lack capacity, we also want to improve commercial certainty for donees and third parties who transact using the LPA.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Currently, section 16 of the MCA protects a donee or any third party who transacted with the donee, if they genuinely did not know that the LPA has not been validly created.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: An LPA could be invalidly created, for example, if the donee handling property and affairs is an undischarged bankrupt at the point when the LPA was made.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The third party transacting with the donee may not know of the donee's bankruptcy, which renders the LPA invalidly created.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: With this amendment, businesses will have confidence to transact with donees using the LPAs as there would be sufficient commercial certainty.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: And this is important because this will, in turn, help the persons who have lost mental capacity to access needed services.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We do want to improve the operations of the OPG to serve the public better.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We are grateful to all those who made suggestions on how to do this.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We have already made some changes based on feedback received, involving the simplifying of the LPA form.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: However, there are other improvements that require changes to the MCA.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: First, we have seen a sharp rise in the volume of LPAs registered with us.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We expect this trend to continue as the population ages and as awareness increases.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The Assistant Public Guardian will exercise all the powers of the PG, except the power of delegation.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The Assistant Public Guardian will be an MSF officer.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Second, we also anticipate that the cases which the OPG has to investigate will become more complex, especially when fraud and financial exploitation have allegedly been committed against a donor with significant and different types of assets.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The auditor appointed by the PG must be a public accountant registered under the Accountants Act.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: When the MCA was first enacted, the PG Board was created to review the way in which the PG's functions were discharged and to report to the Minister.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: This was something new to us and, to my knowledge, no board was ever set up in Singapore previously to specifically supervise the work of a public officer.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: But given that the MCA was an important and a new piece of legislation modelled after the English Mental Capacity Act, we thought it would be prudent to also follow England's practice of having a Board as well.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The Chairman of the PG Board has now recommended to me that the existing Board be replaced with an administrative Advisory Panel.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: As OPG has reached a level of maturity in its operations, he noted that in 2012, even England's PG Board too, was dissolved after being in existence for about five years.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Even as we replace the PG Board with an Advisory Panel, I think it is important to ensure that there are adequate checks and balances.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: First, the PG, like any other public officer in the Ministry, will continue to be accountable to the Minister.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Appeals against decisions made by the PG can be made to the Minister.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Ultimately, a judicial review and appeal through the Courts remain an option.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: At this juncture, I wish to place on record our thanks to the PG Board for its contributions during these six years.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: They have guided the OPG in the implementation of the MCA and were instrumental in establishing OPG's links with the medical, legal and financial sectors.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: I mentioned earlier that the amendments introduced by this Bill will be complemented by policy initiatives that do not require legislative amendments.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: One such initiative involves helping families caring for adult children with intellectual disabilities.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: It is not easy to bring up a child with intellectual disabilities, especially if the caregivers themselves are getting older.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: An MSF officer told me about an elderly couple in their 70s.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: They have two children with intellectual disabilities, who are in their 30s and 40s.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Their father is a lorry driver, their mother a full-time caregiver.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: They worry about their children's welfare when both of them are no longer around.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: They could will their assets to their children, but who will manage it for their benefit?

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Their case is urgent because they are no longer young.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: In fact, I think for many parents who have children with intellectual disabilities, this is one of their main areas of concern.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We have been working hard to address the concerns of these parents.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: This non-profit trust company enables parents to set aside money for their child in a trust account, so that the trust money will be used for the child's care needs when they, as parents, are no longer around.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Money placed in the trust will be administered according to a care plan drawn up by the parents with the help of SNTC.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: This elderly couple signed up straightaway after hearing about the SNTC.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: They shared with us that their minds are definitely more at ease now, as SNTC will use their savings to implement their children's care plan after they pass on.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We want to encourage more parents to make use of this service.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The second thing we are doing is to help parents who have children with special needs to obtain deputyship orders more easily.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We have piloted a project with MINDS for parents of MINDS students to obtain deputyship orders.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Three cases have obtained Court orders so far.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The parents are grateful for the help extended.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: They initially hesitated due to concerns about cost and complexity of the process.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: But they realised that their fears were unfounded.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Immediately after the Court hearing was over, one set of parents came out of the courtroom and thanked everyone involved.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: In another case, the whole family got involved.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: While the parents became deputies, the MINDS student's two older brothers who were in their 20s, became successor deputies.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: As successor deputies, they could take over from their parents should the need arise.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: It is a mirror for all of us.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: It reflects the way we want to live, across the different phases of our lives and across the generations.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: How we treat our parents and family members; how we ourselves want to be treated with respect, with dignity; and when we are no longer the man or woman we once were, how we want the younger generation to step in to hold our hands and help us along.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Not in the direction that they want, but to respect the decisions that we, in our better days, had decided for ourselves.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: To this end, I urge more Singaporeans to think about their future, make plans and do up an LPA.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: This will help make the care-giving journey easier for your family members.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: This mirror also reflects on the professional communities.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: But the MCA can only contain so much.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: What is our collective understanding about the duty owed to the elderly and to respect the wishes of the mentally incapacitated among us?

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: What is our joint action on the policy initiatives and family and community effort?

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The most vulnerable members in our society – the individuals who lack mental capacity − are often the most invisible.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Our duty is to protect them, to respect their wishes and to enable them to live with dignity.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Persons can appoint donees in advance to make decisions on their behalf should they lose capacity.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The Act provided for the Court to appoint deputies for those who have lost capacity.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It further enables parents of children with intellectual disabilities to appoint deputies to oversee welfare and other matters relating to the child.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: This is but only a small percentage of a larger group of Singaporeans who ought to make use of the provisions of the MCA.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The urgency is especially high for three groups of people.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: One, families, especially those with sole breadwinners who, due to injury or sudden deaths, leave their families helpless; Two, persons at risk of losing mental capacity due to age.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There is an estimated 450,000 Singaporeans above the age of 65 in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In my Kampong Glam constituency, I have witnessed the challenges of households where elderly residents lose their mental capacity and no prior arrangements were made for proxy decision-makers.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: As a result, much time and money are expended to ensure the affected elderly receive the needed care and support.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Where property and finance are involved, the administrative hassle led to unnecessary anxiety and resentment, sometimes, resentment of those left behind.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The third group who ought to make use of the MCA provisions are families with special needs children.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Now, they should not be limited to only those with intellectual disabilities.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: These families with children who are deemed to lack the capacity to make significant life decisions are in need of deputies to act on their behalf.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The five areas are: (a) more protection of vulnerable donors; (b) cost of MCA applications and services; (c) families of children with special needs; (d) more resources for administration, education and outreach for the OPG; and (e) the amendment to dissolve the Public Guardian Board First, on the protection of vulnerable donors.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I am concerned with the clause in the current MCA which specifies the qualifications of a donee to simply be at least 21 years old and a non-bankrupt when the LPA is signed.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We can learn more from the highly publicised case of Mdm Chung Khin Chun versus her former tour guide, Yang Yin.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is also appalling that Yang could do as he pleased in his apparently calculated dissipation of Madam Chung's assets in the years before he was arrested.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Next, on the cost of MCA applications and services.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In addition to the application fees to the OPG which are currently kindly waived by the Ministry, there are three costs for which I am asking for better cost management: (a) the remuneration payable for the deputyship and doneeship services for the professional services introduced in the amendments of this Bill; (b) the cost incurred for getting an updated medical report in the course of an MCA application; and (c) the fees payable to the lawyers for work done in explaining to the applicant, drafting the necessary papers and other disbursements.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Next, on families with children with special needs.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I wish to speak on behalf of the many concerned families with children, young and old, with special needs, being a parent myself and an activist in this community.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There is a full continuum of special needs, with different persons manifesting varying degrees of mental capacity.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Families with more severe needs find challenges as they navigate through the sea of uncertainty when their children become adults and many continue to need their families' supervision.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Last year, a group of parents with special needs children wrote to me to share their fears and anxieties about their children who are past the age of 21 with no appointed deputies.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: A mother mentioned that her global-developmentally-delayed daughter needed a treatment that requires general anaesthesia (GA).

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Neither could her parents sign on her behalf because they had not been appointed as her deputy.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Closer to home, an adult with special needs whom I personally know was in need of a wisdom tooth surgery which requires GA as well.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Similarly, the parent was informed by the staff that for an operation that required a GA procedure, she must produce an LP before the young adult could go for the surgery.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The young adult is technically not intellectually disabled – his IQ is above 70 but he has moderate autism.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I confirmed yesterday that the young man has still not gone for his surgery.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: He probably has gotten used to the pain.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: This father could not comprehend why it would be so cumbersome and costly to have himself, as a father, continue to make decisions for his daughter.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: A family residing in my constituency came to ask for my help several times.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The elder sister of a man with severe mental disability wanted me to help appeal for a rental flat from HDB for both of them.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: However, the pace is a tad too slow, in my opinion, and does not include adults above the age of 21 for whom their parents could no longer act on their behalf.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There are many of such families who continue to live in worry and anxiety.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In cases where medical treatment is involved and deputies' consent needed, time is also not on their side and the person with special needs sometimes suffer their physical pain in silence.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Although the law permits healthcare professionals to act in a patient's "best interest" and not requiring consent from a deputy if there is none, there appears to be a lack of awareness and fear of liability on the part of the medical fraternity to perform major procedures on this group.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In this regard, I would strongly recommend that the Ministry take three actions.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: One, further simplify the process of application of deputyship for persons with special needs to cut down both costs and administration.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is not true that only persons with intellectual disabilities need proxy decision-makers.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: One way is to engage and resource the special schools or the major disability organisations to be part of this application process and validate the need for deputyship.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Two, appoint co-ordinating agencies, such as SG-Enable, the National Council of Social Services and/or the Agency for Integrated Care, to promote awareness, educate and provide the required legal and financial assistance for an application under the MCA.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Next, Madam, on more resources for administration, education and outreach work done by the OPG.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The savings resulting from a proper management of affairs when one loses capacity far outweigh the initial cost.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Many more Singaporeans need to come on board this bus and, hence, the OPG has its work cut out for it.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Related parties, such as property agents, HDB frontline officers and healthcare personnel, must be educated, too.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The OPG needs to be future-ready and work on new digital services so that users can more easily access their services.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The UK, for instance, already has its digital LPA services, which allow users to apply for LPAs online, anytime and anywhere.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We need to cater to that group, too, and provide better, faster and cheaper services.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Lastly, on the proposed amendments that repeal the provision for the Public Guardian Board and remove the need to make an annual report on the discharge of the PG's functions, Madam, the OPG under Mr Richard Magnus had performed a commendable job.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: He and his team have built a strong network with the Law Society, College of Family Physicians, CPF Board, grassroots and social service agencies.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Free postage was negotiated with SingPost and the Ministry had waived the application fees for a period to encourage more sign-ups.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The Board has also done an excellent job, no doubt due to its broad network and wisdom.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I feel that it is still early days to dissolve the Board and retire the members.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There is merit to have a Board that provides the external inputs and supervision.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Our Asian culture is such that conversations regarding end-of-life matters are not common.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There are mounting challenges in translating the policies of the OPG to the ground.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: With that, in conclusion, I want to thank the Board and the OPG for running a good race in the last five years, and I look forward to more good years.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Bill will allow professionals to become donees and the Court-appointed deputies under the Act.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It also gives the Court additional powers to manage cases where a donee's or a deputy's powers may need to be revoked, restricted or suspended.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While the benefits of LPAs are clear, the risks have also been painfully clear in recent years.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Vulnerable persons may sign away their rights to property to persons who have unduly influenced them.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Besides the well-publicised case involving a wealthy widow, which Minister mentioned earlier, I have received feedback from residents concerned that a family member may have appointed someone outside the family as his attorney.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In these cases, it is foreseeable that some time down the road, when the LPA is activated due to mental incapacity, the attorney and the family may have disagreements and disputes over how the person should be cared for or his properties dealt with.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I am not saying that a person is not entitled to appoint someone outside the family as an attorney.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Indeed, I totally agree that there may be very good reasons why a person may not want a family member to be his attorney and may not want the family to know of such an appointment.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, currently, all that is needed is for a standard form to be filled up by the person and issued by a doctor or lawyer who may not have any prior knowledge of the person or his circumstances.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To illustrate, I am told that under a well-intentioned ground initiative, large groups of heartland residents were organised to make LPAs at the Ministry issued by persons who had not met them before.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Earlier, the Minister mentioned that the LPA Information Sheet is being amended to encourage donors to inform loved ones of the making of the LPA.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The objection would then need to be assessed by the PG or the Court before the LPA can be registered.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Such a regime would enable LPAs granted in controversial circumstances to be flagged out early before the LPAs take effect.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This potentially prevents the registration of unsound LPAs before the donee takes charge of the properties of the donor.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Moreover, the objection to the registration of the LPA will likely be made when the donor is still mentally lucid and can give invaluable assistance to the PG or the Court to determine if the LPA should be registered or not.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: From what I gather, the Government did not see the need to retain this feature as it was always open to the donor to notify someone if he wished to.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Nevertheless, my view is that it is good to ensure that the donor is always asked whether he wants someone to be notified so that he will direct his mind to that question specifically.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If this is adopted, we will still be respecting the donor's wishes – he can decide whether he wants to notify someone else or not.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I next move on to deputies who may need to be appointed by the Court after a person has become mentally incapacitated.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Their concern is about the legal cost associated with such applications.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For instance, parents of mentally-incapacitated children need a Court Order to act for their children once they attain adulthood.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is clear that these parents will continue to care for their children with or without a Court Order.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In January this year, the Ministry said it was still working with the Family Justice Courts and MINDS on how to simplify the paperwork and process in such cases.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This review has been going on for many months already.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Is the Ministry able to confirm or estimate when this review will be completed?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Earlier, the Minister explained the rationale for clause 11, on why the Public Guardian Board was being abolished.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Currently, section 34 of the Act provides for the PG to make annual reports to the Minister about the discharge of his duties, and I believe these reports are uploaded on the website of the OPG.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Could the Ministry explain why this section is being repealed?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: How would this affect the public accountability of the PG?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I recognise that this is not for lack of trying.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Ministry had made concerted efforts to raise public awareness.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There were regular media coverage and public education efforts to get more Singaporeans to appoint donees to make decisions on their behalf in the event that they lose mental capacity in the future.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I have seen colourful, full-page advertisements on the LPA in both the English and Chinese newspapers.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Despite all these efforts, the general awareness is still not high, especially among the elderly.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Even those who are aware of the scheme are not pro-active in signing up.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Others assume erroneously that, by default, their spouses and children will be able to make decisions on their behalf.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Yet others are superstitious and prefer to avoid this topic altogether.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Considering our rapidly ageing population, it is important to get more Singaporeans to do their LPAs.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With longer lifespans, the probability of loss of mental capacity in the final years is higher and will affect a greater number of people.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Without appointed donees, our Courts will have to hear more applications by affected families to appoint deputies when their loved ones lose their mental capacities.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Not only will this be a strain on the resources of the families during a difficult period, it will also tax our public resources.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Much more importantly, without appointed donees, the welfare of the elderly will be compromised as care and financial arrangements will inevitably be delayed.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Allow me to share a real-life example to highlight the hardships a family went through due to the absence of an LPA.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And this is a case from my constituency.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: An elderly gentleman fell ill and, after a prolonged stay in hospital, he was discharged as the doctors were unable to do more for him.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: His condition was bad but he hung in there and his children arranged for various medical equipment to be installed at home, which were quite costly.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: He had his own HDB flat and funds in a few bank accounts.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: His wife passed away a few years ago.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Unfortunately, his children could not draw upon the funds in his bank accounts and so they used their own money.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: His children also had to support young children of their own.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: After a few months, they decided to seek help at a Meet-the-People session because the financial strain was increasingly harder to bear.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, this process is definitely more troublesome and time-consuming than if an LPA was done earlier.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The first target group we must work with is the elderly.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many of them are not aware of LPAs.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We should have more publicity in mother tongues, including dialects, as we have done for the Pioneer Generation scheme.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our PGAs can explain the implications and the importance of selecting the right donees.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The third non-legislative initiative I would like to propose is to get registered medical practitioners who are certificate issuers to put up big, elderly-friendly signs indicating that they can witness and certify LPAs at their clinics.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The OPG should design and issue these uniform signs.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Compared to registered psychiatrists or practising lawyers who are also approved certificate issuers, doctors are much more accessible to the general public.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am sure most people will feel more comfortable approaching their regular neighbourhood GPs to get their LPAs done.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These signs will also act as visual prompts to their patients and remind them to do their LPAs.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Next, I would like to refer to the amendment to allow the Court to temporarily suspend a donee's or deputy's powers in the absence of a pending Court application.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Obviously, prevention is very much better than cure.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Therefore, the process of selecting suitable donees or deputies should be rigorous.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is far better to choose a suitable one than to have to go through the process of getting rid of an unsuitable donee or deputy.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For example, if the donee is not closely related or is unrelated to the donor despite the donor being married with children, would red flags be raised?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would the PG arrange for an interview with the donor to clarify suspicious applications, follow up with his family members, and provide counselling and advisory services?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I believe strongly that the family should be the first line of support but, in the event that family members are found not to be suitable to be deputies, how does the Court decide on which professional deputies to be appointed?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And for deputies who have been suspended, are their names made known in a register which can be accessible by the public?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I appreciate the Minister's response to my questions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I recognise that it is necessary to allow such appointments as some persons who are subject to the Act may not want their family members to take charge of their personal matters or be their donee or deputy, or some people simply do not have a suitable relative or friend to be their donee or deputy.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The criteria should go beyond just allowing people to qualify as professional donees and deputies by merely being members of certain professions, say, for example, doctors, lawyers, accountants or even social workers, or even community groups.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And I will also extend that to trust companies.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will the Minister please share with the House more details of the criteria and training for professional donees and deputies?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will the Minister please explain how the Ministry intends to ensure that the fees be kept affordable?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How does the Ministry expect the Courts to determine the remuneration under the proposed new section 24(8A)(b)?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In any case, there may also be some people who will not be able to afford a professional donee or deputy and, at the same time, are not able to find a suitable person to do it for free.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am indeed, encouraged by the Minister's opening remarks on this issue.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will allow the PG to intervene in suitable cases where the donee and deputy may not be carrying out his duties properly and the interests of the persons which the Act seeks to protect can be better safeguarded.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They should, in fact, make it easier and less costly for any layperson to make such applications directly.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, instead of using formal Court applications, summonses and affidavits, we can also consider using appropriate layman-friendly application forms, supported by statutory declarations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The current affidavit template can be converted to such a form.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Perhaps, we can really think out of the box here.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If we can simplify the application, the legal fees can be further reduced.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Court filing fees for all documents can also be reduced by not having it pegged to the existing Court filing fees for Court summonses and affidavits.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I would also suggest that even for the present regime, a detailed checklist can be published on the relevant website of the likely issues that need to be addressed in each application and the depth at which the issues need to be addressed.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will help lay people to better understand the requirements of the application readily.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: With modernisation, our smaller nuclear families, "empty nest" syndrome, singlehood and widowed spouses from the longer duration of lifespans, especially for women, we have all these that are pointing in the right direction towards this updated Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: When there is a lack of our first line of support, which is the family, then donees and deputies will play a useful role.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: However, they have to be adequately selected, prepared and appointed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: This can then be a checking mechanism and a safeguard, especially for those who really do not have family nor other persons for support.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Moreover, we can expect many of these persons to be in the more advanced stages of their lives and we do not want them to be taken for a ride or be taken advantage of by unscrupulous parties.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: I, therefore, support the suggested aid for those who deserve it and also a kind of a Legal Aid mechanism mentioned earlier.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The IMCA can make representation on the person's wishes, feelings and beliefs and bring these to the attention of decision makers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: I am not saying that we adopt this wholesale.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: But, in it, there are, indeed, gaps and limitations that perhaps consideration of some modifications or a customised version might be useful for our setting.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: It will also be useful for such a list to denote areas of specialisation of the personnel, such as whenever it is related to personal affairs, property, welfare or financial matters.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: This will reduce waste of time and expected changes that may need to be done later on if the wrong person is appointed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: This may require it to be tagged to a suitable market rate, but with some degree of flexibility.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: But the main aim would be not to overburden such affected families, who may already be financially over-stretched.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: For those with mental incapacity who are institutionalised, for example, in nursing homes or attached to a VWO, can there be consideration for a "package offering" for them, especially for those with no next-of-kin and families?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Importantly, also, there must be some guidelines to exempt or exclude those staff who are directly involved in the care of these clients from being their deputies for reasons of conflict of interest.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: On dealing with requests for medical reports for such cases, can we have a systematic algorithm streamlined, clearly drawn up, because I find that this can actually be a rate-limiting step or factor in most cases?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: When the Court suspends the donee's or deputy's powers in the absence of a pending Court application, can the Minister share with us the timeline within which this is acceptable before it needs to be considered void?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: This would be an interesting point as we are facing the onslaught of an ageing population.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: One more point, for a patient who has severe mental health disorder – I am not referring to the mild or moderate spectrum where symptoms can be controlled by drugs and therapy and they can function normally in society, the family and at work, which affects the insight and cognitive capabilities of persons – can they be covered under the MCA, and I assume they would, of course, need their medical specialists to verify and certify the severity of the illness in this case?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: And, of course, need to be given a case-by-case consideration.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Any decision made under this Act for a person lacking mental capacity must be made in his or her best interest.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: (In Malay):   Mdm Speaker, in amending this Act, we can do more to share information with the public.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: This is because many are unsure and unaware about the application of this Act.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: We must explain its details in a way that can be easily understood.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Many people within our Malay community will not be able to understand the facts in its present form and, because of that, the number of people making use of this Act is very small.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: If we are required to provide data and information that are 10 pages long, many will not even want to do it.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: With the rising number of singles and increased number of elderly living alone, it is timely to introduce professional donees and deputies, as this group of people might not have family members who can help them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There are, however, a number of issues I would like to raise.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We must continue to focus on family support as the priority.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister also clarify if all professional donees will be registered with the PG since not all donees might be deputies?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, on section 25A(2) which states that "The Public Guardian may register a person as a professional deputy upon being satisfied that the person meets all the prescribed criteria".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As mentioned, now we have a rising number of singles and an increased number of elderly living alone.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What is the Government's plan to encourage this group of people, especially those without family members, to make the LPA?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is difficult for the elderly to understand what an LPA is, let alone how to apply for one.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Could the Pioneer Generation Office perhaps help with the outreach and provide advice to them on LPAs?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But for the elderly group of people mentioned earlier, I doubt these measures will result in an increase in LPA applications from this group.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We need to really reach out to them and make them aware of the LPAs in the first place.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Also, as previously mentioned by other Members, the professional donees and deputies will clearly be charging for their services.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister give an idea of what the estimated costs will be?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As the demographics of people who might need this professional service will tend to be single, elderly and without family support, I am concerned that the use of this service might further result in a financial strain on them as they might already have limited financial resources.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand that MSF does already, on a case-by-case basis, waive application fees for LPAs for those who cannot afford the fees.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will MSF also consider working closely with VWOs in the social service sector to develop the professional deputies and donees industry?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Working with the non-profit sector, rather than the for-profit sector in this case, might result in lower professional fees and better services.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Staff members or volunteers of these VWOs may already be providing services to the individuals and will already be familiar with their needs and preferences.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, as the Minister has mentioned, parents of children with intellectual disability have to apply to the Court to appoint themselves as deputies for their children.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will MSF consider allowing parents of children with intellectual disability to be deputies by default?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I believe this will help them save valuable time, energy and financial resources.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand that MSF – and the Minister has mentioned it earlier as well – has reviewed this recommendation and has decided against it.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is instead working on simplifying the process.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I note this proposal will address the emerging needs of the ageing population in Singapore, especially with the increasing number of elderly singles or elderly couples who do not have children.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: These elderly may not have next-of-kin to be their donees or deputies and can refer to a registered group of professionals or assistants.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In addition to such scenarios where no next-of-kin is available, I believe that the services of these professionals can also be extended to situations even where there may be next-of-kin present.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I acknowledge that one of the key principles of the MCA is that the family is the first line of support but also note the community has its part to play.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The role of a donee or a deputy can be very challenging.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It may be that the available family member is not the best person to help carry out the role, for example, if the family or next-of-kin is overseas.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In respect of the appointment of deputy, it may also be that there are disputing family members and one way to avoid the impasse amongst them would be to engage a neutral professional.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I know of situations where the finalisation of an appointment of a deputy for an individual is delayed because of disagreements amongst family members.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I would propose that it should be, as it would provide options for the family and the Court in appropriate circumstances.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The role of a donee or deputy is a serious obligation and may require the professional to make complex decisions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In particular, as the professional deputy will have to be registered with the PG, there is a need to ensure the high standards of the professionals as the public will come to rely on the register, expect that the professionals have been screened and can be trusted.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There should be a framework to ensure adequate training as well as proper guidelines and supervision of both professional donees and deputies.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I now move to my second point regarding access to the public in creating the LPA and obtaining an order for the appointment of a deputy.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: A pertinent issue to address is whether costs will be an impediment and this is a common issue which has been raised by a few of my hon parliamentary colleagues.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: At this juncture, I would also like to declare that, as a lawyer, I have assisted clients in their applications for appointments of deputies.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: With the introduction of professional donees and deputies who will be remunerated for their services, there is an issue as to whether there will be guidelines on the appropriate costs to be charged by these professionals.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In the case of an appointment of a deputy, typically, lawyers are involved and parties have to incur legal costs.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The other aspect of improving access of these processes to the public is public education and the simplification of processes.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In respect of the LPA, although there has been much public education on its importance and processes, there is still some way to go in helping more people get the LPA done early.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: To this end, I think efforts can be ramped up at the grassroots level or through volunteers, as alluded to by my colleague Ms Joan Pereira earlier, like the PGAs, to facilitate the registration of the LPA.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It may be necessary to bring the process down to the masses, such as making the arrangements for obtaining the appointment with the Certificate Issuer and facilitating the completion and submission of the LPA at community touch-points, such as the CC or CC events.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I would also like to highlight that the applicant of an LPA would also have to incur costs in obtaining the endorsement of a Certificate Issuer.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I note that these costs are not prescribed or controlled by the OPG.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: While the cost may be relatively low for standard situations, this may still be a significant sum for low-income Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In respect of the appointment of deputies, many have commented that the process can be complicated, long-drawn and fairly costly.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: As a lawyer, I understand that the process needs to be sufficiently rigorous, as an order to appoint a deputy is a very serious one.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: A deputy will be given powers to make decisions on behalf of an individual who can no longer make his or her own decisions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Measures need to be put in place to ensure that proper checks are made, sufficient information is given to the Court and all questions are answered.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This could explain why legal costs can be quite high.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, I believe there can be some effort to assist low to middle income families with this.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This is especially so if they have had to spend much of their income on medical expenses.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: These efforts will go a long way in facilitating the process and alleviating the hardship for many families.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: These proposals are a step in the right direction, with sufficient safeguards to protect and serve the public.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With an ageing population and the likely association of cognitive impairment with illness or just ageing, it is timely that the amendments seek to better protect the interests of persons who may lose their mental capacity.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The amendments take into account changing realities in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: People are living longer and we are also seeing an increasing number of elderly singles or elderly living with their aged spouses without children.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The amendments will enable the elderly who may not have family members who could act as suitable donees or deputies to appoint professional donees and deputies to make advance plans for themselves in relation to decisions on their personal welfare, property and finances.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: How can we ensure that this stays affordable?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Are there regulations for professional donees and deputies and what are the measures to ensure that they have the qualifications to be able to perform the very complex roles that they are entrusted with?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This will enable the Court to revoke the donee or deputy if they have been convicted of an offence involving dishonesty or fraud against another person and not just the person lacking mental capacity.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This is an important improvement and enhances protection for the donors.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The current Act only allows the Court to revoke a donee's or deputy's powers if he is likely to act outside of the authority given to him, or is behaving against the best interest of the person who lacks mental capacity.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This is an improvement on the current situation in which an application to Court has to be made to remove a deputy or donee for the Court to do so.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This is to protect the wealth of the person who is mentally incapacitated, while investigations are on-going.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Hence, while these amendments enhance the protection, it will still require the Court to respect the decisions made by individuals when they have the mental capacity to do so, even if these decisions may seem unusual, unreasonable or unwise to some of us.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We must, however, recognise that there may be undue influence that could impact a person's ability to make the right choice for himself.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This will support and help them make the right choices for themselves when appointing donees.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This Bill strives to strike a very difficult balance, a balance between enhancing protection and making it less onerous for individuals, while they still have the mental capacity, to plan and make decisions for themselves with regard to their personal welfare and private wealth.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This Bill is part of our evolution in dealing with the rising challenge of mental illness.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The predecessor to the MCA was the Mental Disorders and Treatment Act (MDTA).

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The MDTA allowed the Court to intervene where it was established that the person had lost his mental capacity.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This obviously created problems because, usually, when that happened and the Court action took place, there would be the inevitable dispute on the formation of the Committee.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The MCA evolved in the process and allowed the creation of the LPA.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The LPA is a provision that empowers people to make decisions while they are still mentally healthy on who should determine their affairs in the event they lose their mental capacity.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The roles and responsibilities of people appointed under the LPA, the donees, are very wide-ranging.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: They include matters relating to the personal welfare of the person, which includes sensitive topics like where the person will stay, what medical treatment he will get, whether surgery is opted for.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: They will also deal with the property and affairs of the person and this also includes sensitive matters, such as whether or not they keep the place he is staying at, whether or not the flat should be sold, how the expenses should be managed.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It is only right that all these very sensitive matters are dealt with by a donee chosen when the person still has his mental faculties.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I would also suggest the class of persons to be treated as professional donees – it has not been set out in the Bill and I believe this will be set out in subsequent legislation or by guidance given by the Minister – my suggestion for the professional donees would be to define this class as broadly as possible.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I believe different considerations apply for professional donees and deputies.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Professional donees would, ultimately, be people who are selected while the person still has mental capacity.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In this regard, describing this class broadly would allow a person to have more choices as to who he picks as a professional donee.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It gives individuals a chance to appoint professionals where they believe professionals may be more reliable than family members.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In practice, being a lawyer, one sees many unhappy situations where family members are involved in personal affairs and this can be for many number of reasons arising from differences of opinion as to how the person should be treated, to even more sensitive matters such as where there is a great deal of expense to be determined, the family members may have other vested interests in preserving the assets or the property, as opposed to taking care of the welfare of the person.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, where there are all these sensitive trade-offs to be made, it is sometimes helpful to have someone who is outside the family to make the decision.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For this reason, I think professional donees are necessary.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is also a system that had some practice in the UK, and I think there would be good guidance for us from there, too.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: My other suggestion for the professional donees is this.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: People can download forms, they can execute them before lawyers or selected doctors, and this is relatively straightforward.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I would also suggest these fees begin only after the professional donee starts managing affairs.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The more we standardise these processes, the easier it will be for the user.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Obviously, the high-income users or people with higher net worth can get professional advice and vary from the standard form.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But for most ordinary people, it would be helpful to have standard forms for the appointment of professional donees.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Professional deputies are somewhat different creatures from the professional donee.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, typically, professional deputies are appointed only in situations where a person has not actually executed an LPA.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, this comes in where a person has not had a chance to make a choice.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I did a straw poll of some of my parliamentary colleagues and I am sad to report that, myself included, none of us has executed our LPAs yet.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, my guess is that there will be a very large class of people who have not executed LPAs.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: What this means is that the professional deputies will be increasingly important because the reality is that, despite all our best intentions, most people will not make this decision beforehand, and this decision is going to end up before the Court.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The professional deputies will arise only where a deputy has not been appointed.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, typically, if a person has some loving family members, they will apply to Court to be deputies.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There will be no fees involved, and this should be a relatively straightforward process.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, if there is a dispute between the family, then the disputing family members may also appear before the Court at this time.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: They will have their dispute before the Court and the Court will make them decide whether to appoint the deputy or if it wishes to appoint a professional deputy.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It is in these kinds of situation where the Court's judgment would be extremely important.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Court's judgment will invariably be based on what they believe will be in the best interest of the person.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And obviously, the Courts, quite rightly, have a wide discretion in this.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There is another reason the professional deputy is very important – why this list should be kept tight.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is because once a person is on the list of professional deputies, first of all, that would also be a signal to people appointing professional donees that this is a potential person that they can go to, if they do not have any family contacts.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, in that sense, the list of professional deputies is a signal to the public that this is a list of approved people that you can appoint as professional donees.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There is no general provision that allows all and sundry to apply under the Act if they feel that there is abuse.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, for example, the good-natured neighbour, if he were to discover abuse, he may make a report to the PG but he has no right to commence any action in his own name under the Bill.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Others do have a right under section 38(2) of the Act to get permission from the Court to start an application.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, there is a two-step process for them.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But this two-step process may take some time.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The other matter is the manner in which the Court will exercise its discretion when deciding whether or not one of the people that is not designated in section 38(1) would have permission to commence action.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The MCA very helpfully sets out the criterion which the Court will consider in section 38(3).

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It says that the Court will look at the applicant's connection to the person, the reasons for the application, the benefit to the person to whom the application relates and whether the benefits can be achieved in any other way.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: What this means again is that a person who will get no personal benefit from taking an action under this Bill, may have a more limited right to commence action under this Bill.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The PG has power under section 38(1) itself.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
