text: But if this is the intended way, meaning that the PG is going to be the main person investigating abuse, then the PG will need more resources to do that.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: These are points that we will definitely take into consideration when we look at the regulatory framework.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The inputs today have been quite useful and we do urge Members to continue to provide us with more details should you have other suggestions.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Members have supported the introduction of "professional donees" and "professional deputies".

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: I think we all recognise that given the trends going forward, this is something that we all need.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Members have also raised concerns, fair concerns and things that we were also pre-occupied with when preparing these amendments.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: First, several Members, including Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef, Mr Louis Ng, Ms Rahayu Mahzam, Mr Dennis Tan and Ms Jessica Tan highlighted that there must be proper rules and also training for professional donees and deputies.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We need to make sure that not only are they qualified but they are also suitable.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: I am not sure whether it is easy as Mr Dennis Tan has suggested, in terms of attitudes, to assess that.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: But those are factors that highlighted the importance of making sure that due diligence is put in place to pick the right donees and deputies.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We do intend to put in place a robust set of criteria for those who wish to register with the OPG as a professional deputy.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: And, certainly, what is important is that we are also looking into training programmes to ensure competency.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Through that process, through training programmes, possibly, we may also detect if the individuals are not suitable, and we may then not register them accordingly.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Mr Louis Ng wished to clarify if all professional donees must register with the PG.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: But this is not to say they will not be regulated.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The first comprises persons who have been registered with the PG as professional deputies.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Simply, they can already act as donees and deputies under the MCA today.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: They are tightly regulated by the Monetary Authority of Singapore(MAS) under the Trust Companies Act.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef and Mr Louis Ng asked if nursing homes and VWOs can serve as deputies to their clients.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We prefer that they do not do so.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Doing so could create a potential conflict of interest where they can decide to procure and charge for their own services.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: It would really be better if an independent professional deputy was appointed, if needed.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Second, several Members, in fact, a number of Members, have expressed concern about the fees professional donees and deputies may charge.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We think that controlling fees right at the onset might not be the best way to keep prices affordable.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: A fee cap could remove the incentive for service providers to charge competitive rates and stunt the growth of services for differing needs and circumstances.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: As Members realise, every individual comes with a very different context and there might be different types of services required, thereby, requiring different charges.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: It may also deter competent service providers from entering if the fee cap is set wrongly, especially.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Moreover, with regard to Mr Dennis Tan's question, the remuneration a professional deputy may claim also depends on what the Court deems fit in his case.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: So, the Court will also have to apply itself to assess whether the remuneration is appropriate or not.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Mr Vikram Nair asked if there will be standardised LPA forms and fee guidelines for professional donees.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: As the donor may wish to give specific powers to the donee, we are not sure if it is advisable to have standardised forms.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The donor and the donee should also be free to decide on the fee arrangements.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: After all, this is when the donor has his full mental faculties and he should be able to decide for himself what he is prepared to pay and what are the arrangements he would like to put in place with the donee.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Third, Ms Joan Pereira asked how the Court would decide on which professional deputy to appoint.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: When a professional deputy applies to Court, the Court would have to evaluate, based on the circumstances of the case, whether it is appropriate to appoint that professional as the person's deputy.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: In addition, as Ms Rahayu Mahzam noted, the Court could also appoint a professional deputy if it is satisfied that the significant others are unwilling, unable or unsuitable to act, especially if there are family disputes.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: On a related point on safeguards, Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef also asked if an Independent Mental Capacity Advocate – or the IMCA – service could be considered in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: This is an advocacy service provided in the UK to those without deputies, donees and family support.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We did consider this quite carefully when we first introduced the MCA.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We believed then and we still do now, that we have sufficiently protected mentally incapacitated persons.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Section 7 of the MCA allows for professionals, such as doctors and caregivers, to act in the best interest of the incapacitated person.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: They can consult those who know the mentally-incapacitated persons to better understand their wishes.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: In this way, we enable professionals and caregivers to care for the incapacitated confidently, while avoiding unnecessary costs and complexity.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Where it is really necessary, professional deputies may be appointed.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Members supported the amendments to enable pre-emptive action to protect individuals from abuse by their proxy decision-makers, but had some concerns.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: I will address the concerns, but let me first reiterate that the fundamental principle of the MCA is to respect the decisions of a person who has mental capacity, and this is something that Ms Jessica Tan had also highlighted.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: It is important for us to remember that we may not always agree with the decision, we may think the decision is unwise, but if they still retain their full mental faculties, that is something that we have to respect.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: It is the same way as they make wills, individuals who make wills out of different individuals and we have to respect them.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Ms Joan Pereira and Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef asked about how and how long it would take to suspend an unsuitable donee or deputy.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The process involves preparing an application that is supported by sworn statements from the witnesses, to prove that it is necessary for the Court to suspend the donee's or deputy's powers.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The duration of this process will largely depend on the complexity and evidence provided.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Where there is an urgent need for protection, the OPG will expedite the filing of the Court application and ask the Court to hear their application on an urgent basis.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The order will then continue until the donee or deputy applies to set it aside, or until a further Court order, whichever is earlier.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: If there is a suspension order, the Court may also place limits on what can be withdrawn by the donee or deputy for the day-to-day living and medical expenses of the person without capacity.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: In this same way, the same level of care can be provided as before the suspension order.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Mr Vikram Nair asked if the OPG is resourced to investigate complaints and about access to Courts.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: As to access to Court, apart from PG, concerned others can apply to Court.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: While permission is required for non-family members, the process is similar to that for PG.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Ms Joan Pereira also asked how members of the public will know whether a donee or deputy has been suspended.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: It would also be prudent to request to search Court records for the latest status on the validity of a Court order appointing a deputy.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Ms Denise Phua, Ms Sylvia Lim and Ms Joan Pereira asked if OPG can do more to check LPA applications, particularly for "high-risk" cases.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Ms Sylvia Lim asked if the option to notify main persons could be reinserted into the standard LPA form.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Paradoxically, I fully understand and I agree with the concern, that if the intent of the option was really to protect against undue influence, a donor who is unduly influenced, is very unlikely to notify anyone.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Even if he or she did, he or she probably would not be notifying the correct persons.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: What we hope to do is, in terms of the prompt, to advise them to speak to their family, brief them on their LPA arrangements so that, at least, they can understand.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: This is no guarantee that they would do it, but that is something that we are putting in place.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: OPG checks LPA applications to ensure that they comply with the legal requirements set out in the MCA and Regulations.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: As I have highlighted, OPG typically does not question the donor's choice of donee – whether the donee is a family member, as in most cases, or a professional – because the donor is deemed to have mental capacity.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The donor must also get a certificate issuer to certify that the donor understands the purpose of the LPA and the scope of the authority conferred on donees in the LPA and that no fraud or undue pressure was used to induce the donor to make the LPA.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: As I have shared earlier, each case has its unique circumstances.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We do not believe it is appropriate for the PG to raise red flags just because the donee is a foreigner or not a relative.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The PG should not, I believe, act as an arbiter of another's choices.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Again, just to reiterate, the core principle of the MCA is to respect the choice of a person who has mental capacity.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The registry of the LPAs is a confidential registry, similar to the Wills Registry.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: It would be inappropriate for PG to share information about the donor's LPA with the donor's family members.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: What we can do is to encourage the donor himself to share the information with his family members.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: What we can do and have done is this: to encourage them not just to talk to the family members and, hopefully, in the process, to choose a donee wisely.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The PG will only step in and, rightly so, when the donee is not acting in the donor's best interests and has no one else to intervene.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The MCA also provides for whistle-blower protection to those who report potential abuse.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We want to assure Members that we fully understand the dilemmas that you have brought to bear and because of many of the cases that Members have seen.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: In the vast majority of cases, we do not face the problem but, obviously, these cases, when they do surface, can be quite dramatic and they seize the public imagination.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: But it is a fine balance to strike.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: On the one hand, it is important to respect the individual; on the other hand, we also need to be sufficiently rigorous to protect the individual as well.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Ms Denise Phua expressed concern about the retiring of the PG Board, although the Chairman of the PG Board had made this recommendation.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Ms Sylvia Lim also asked why the Ministry has done away with the requirements for an annual report.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: I want to assure Members that we have considered this very carefully before deciding to make this move and I have explained earlier in my opening speech.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The PG Board was established to scrutinise and to review the way in which the PG's functions were discharged when the MCA was a relatively new piece of legislation.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: With the Board's help, we have improved various internal processes and guidelines for OPG to operate effectively.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The Board also assisted OPG in establishing links, which Members have rightly pointed out, is really important, not only with key stakeholders like the Law Society and College of Family Physicians, but also at the customer front-ends, such as the CPF, the grassroots and many other stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Based on these improvements, the Chairman himself felt that they have achieved the objectives and could be dissolved.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: After examining their proposal thoroughly, I have agreed with the recommendation.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Individuals who suspect that the PG had not discharged his functions in good faith and with reasonable care can make this known to the Minister.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The annual report was submitted by the PG Board to the Minister.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: It accounted primarily for the initiatives and the review of the OPG's activities in the year concerned.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Some may feel that it is better to retain the PG Board so that it can provide constructive feedback.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: However, the idea is that the Advisory Panel, which we are forming, will continue to comprise various respected professionals in the medical, legal, finance and social work sectors.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: I am very sure that they will provide independent and constructive feedback, as they have done so previously when they were a Board.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Members asked how to increase public awareness and accessibility of the LPA and how to reduce the cost in making an LPA or a deputyship order.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Ms Rahayu Mahzam, Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef and Ms Jessica Tan believe that more need to be educated about the LPA and the implications of the appointment and choice of donees.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Ms Joan Pereira, Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef, Mr Louis Ng and Mr Dennis Tan have suggested various ways to raise the awareness and accessibility of the LPA and, especially, in keeping the process simple, which we agree.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: OPG conducts monthly LPA talks at Raffles Place, for example, and will hold talks in mother tongues later this year.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The talks cover the technical aspects of how to make an LPA, the types of powers donees may be given and also the importance of choosing trusted persons to act as donees.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: OPG has also recently produced two videos; one, on the need for an LPA, specifically targeting the elderly; and, the other, on how exactly to apply for the LPA itself.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: These videos have been subtitled in the four languages and would soon be posted on OPG's website and further disseminated.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The OPG's helpline can also handle calls and enquiries in the four official languages.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Basically, the idea is that we will do whatever we can to raise awareness as much as possible, and we do ask Members of this House to support us and assist us in that process.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: On Ms Joan Pereira's and Mr Louis Ng's point that PGAs can play a role – that is something we can definitely consider.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Feedback from the public and the Pioneer Generation Office has been positive.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: They are, indeed, a good resource base that we can draw on, especially to encourage those without family members, to make an LPA.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: While they may appoint close and trusted friends to be their donees, some may also consider appointing a professional donee when the regulatory framework is up.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: As for getting registered medical practitioners to put up signs indicating that they can certify LPAs, we can explore if that is feasible as well.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Applications to register an LPA can now be made by post.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We have also waived the postage charge for a similar two-year period.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We are working closely with the Family Courts to keep the process simple.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: That is something many Members have raised and we fully agree with that.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We welcome suggestions and specific ideas about how we can make it simple because that is really where we should go.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: But, again, I just want to flag out that we do need to find a balance.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Because on the one hand – and I think Ms Rahayu Mahzam raised the point – we want ease and accessibility and, of course, with that, lower cost.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: But at the same time, we do need rigour, because this is an important process and we need to get it right.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: So, these two considerations remain important and we need to find that balance, and Members' inputs would be tremendously helpful on that front.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Regarding the fees that certificate issuers charge, such fees, I believe, are warranted, because of the important role in the LPA-making process and they carry serious, significant legal implications.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Having said that, we will continue to see how best to reduce the cost of making the LPA.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: On the matter of deputyship applications, we agree with Ms Rahayu Mahzam that deputyship is a serious matter and we need to bear this in mind, even as we work with various groups to make the process easier for them to apply for deputyship.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: This is also why, for Mr Louis Ng's question on whether parents with children with intellectual disability can be made "natural deputies", we think that a judicial process is needed.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The Court needs to evaluate the specific matters in which the individual with intellectual disability lacks capability and whether the proposed deputy is suitable to act, even if it is the parent.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: There are also instances where parents may be unsuitable – for instance, parents who are abusive or who have serious illnesses that may impair their own mental capacity.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Ms Denise Phua asked if the deputyship process can be made easier and more accessible, especially for individuals with special needs.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We are certainly making progress in the pilot project with MINDS, which has been completed.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: As for the next steps, which Ms Denise Phua, Ms Sylvia Lim and Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef asked about, we have, as I have mentioned, completed a project and are now working with MINDS to scale up and cover the graduating cohort of MINDS students.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We will also be covering those who have already left school and also those with other forms of intellectual disabilities and autism.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Basically, we are confident and have found it useful and successful and do intend to scale up.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: It will take some time, but we intend to expand it.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We will look into Ms Denise Phua's suggestions to encourage healthcare professionals to act under section 7 of the MCA in the best interest of their patients, without the need for formally-appointed deputies.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: At the same time, we will also look into familiarising healthcare professionals with the medical report required for deputyship and encourage them to set reasonable fees.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: In response to Mr Dennis Tan and also Ms Sylvia Lim, we have completed work with the Family Justice Courts.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We continue to work very closely with them in fact, it has been a very constructive relationship between both parties, because of a lot of inputs that we have been able to gather from both sides.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We are in the process of further simplification of forms and some processes, and this has been implemented in the MINDS pilot.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: However, do continue to give us your suggestions.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: What Members have highlighted has been most useful.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef asked whether a person with severe mental health disorder can be covered under the MCA.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Ms Denise Phua also highlighted that there are others with other conditions that may impair their ability to make decisions for themselves.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The answer is yes, if the severe mental disorder results in mental incapacity.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Someone is considered to lack mental capacity to make a decision if he or she is unable to (a) understand the relevant information; (b) retain the information; (c) weigh the information as part of the decision-making process; or (d) communicate his or her decision.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: If a severe mental disorder or any other condition results in the inability to do one or more of these things, the person would be covered by the MCA.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: There may be cases of fluctuating capacity among those with severe mental health disorders.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: In these cases, a report from a medical practitioner would be needed.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Donees and deputies are not permitted to make or revoke an AMD on behalf of persons without mental capacity.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Once again, thank you very much for all your valuable inputs.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We do encourage Members to continue to provide us with suggestions, ideas and feedback from the public.
